newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania and Hungary leaders sign historic treaty.
newsitem.headline: Romania and Hungary leaders sign historic treaty.

text.p: Romania and Hungary on Monday signed a historic treaty to end a centuries-old rift between the two states amid protests by thousands against President Ion Iliescu's leftist regime.

The pact, signed by Romanian Prime Minister Nicolae Vacaroiu and his Hungarian counterpart Gyula Horn, in Iliescu's presence, should put an end to political sabre-rattling between Bucharest and Budapest.

"The treaty opens a new chapter which ends the era of disputes between Romania and Hungary," Horn said during a ceremony in the ornate local government office in Timisoara, on the border with Yugoslavia and Hungary.
The deal caps five years of tough negotiations over the status of Romania's 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians and its insistence that the pact should guarantee its borders.
"We have witnessed a special event, with deep impact on Romanian-Hungarian relations, and with a European and international impact," Vacaroiu said.

Iliescu said the treaty would enhance regional security and stability, hailing it as a step towards historic reconciliation between the ex-communist neighbours, modelled on the post-war French-German relationship.
"The joint integration of Romania and Hungary into Western structures offers firm guarantees of fostering democracy and economic reform in the two countries," Iliescu said.

As he spoke, some 2,500 anti-government protesters outside the building shouted "Down with Iliescu, down with Vacaroiu". Riot police cordoned off the area to keep the crowd under control and no violence was reported.
Timisoara was the cradle of the December, 1989, popular revolt, which spread like wildfire across Romania, ending 50 years of communism.
Western leaders praised Romania and Hungary for concluding a pact vital for both countries' ambitions to join the European Union and NATO.
Ignoring opposition from nationalists and responding to Western pressure, both states last month agreed a treaty text that sidesteps the most sensitive issues.
The Hungarians dropped demands for ethnic autonomy for the minorities, which had fuelled Romanian fears of a Yugoslav-type secession, in exchange for minority rights guarantees.
French President Jacques Chirac wrote to Iliescu and Horn ahead of Monday's ceremony, praising both sides for their courage to "overcome reflexes of mutual mistrust stemming from a troubled history".
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said the pact would help both nations in their quest for EU membership.
"Romania and Hungary have taken an important step for Europe through their readiness to conduct bilateral relations as good neighbours," Kinkel said in a statement issued in Bonn.
Leaders of Romania's centrist opposition attended Monday's ceremony, but it was boycotted by nationalists of the National Unity Party (PUNR), who said the treaty would jeopardise Romania's integrity.
Ethnic Hungarian leaders were also absent, planning to hold a vigil in the city's Roman-Catholic cathedral later on Monday.
